Bounded Length Confidence Interval for a Median, Distribution Free

Source: R/seq_blci_dfr_median.R
seq_blci_dfr_median.Rd

Given the data collected so far, checks the stopping rule of the purely sequential bounded length confidence interval for a population median when the distribution is not specified (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009). The interval runs between two order statistics of the sample, and observations are collected until its length is at most \(2d\). The quantity estimated is the population median, not the mean.

Usage

seq_blci_dfr_median(x, d, conf_level = 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of the observations collected so far (at least 1; an interval is reported once there are enough for the confidence level, see Details).

d

Half of the largest interval length allowed, in the units of the data: sampling continues until the length of the interval is at most \(2d\). A positive number.

conf_level

The confidence level (default 0.95).

na.rm

Logical; should NA values be removed first? Default TRUE. With FALSE, missing values are an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and these rows:

lower_limit

The order statistic \(X_{(b)}\).

median

The sample median, the point estimate.

upper_limit

The order statistic \(X_{(n-b+1)}\).

interval_length

The upper limit minus the lower limit.

current_n

The number of observations used.

The two limits and the length are NA when there are too few observations for the confidence level. Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE when the interval length is at most \(2d\)); current_n; criterion_n, which is NA because the rule is stated in terms of the interval length and not a target sample size; conf_level; width (the bound \(2d\)); method; min_n (the smallest sample size at which the confidence level can be reached); ranks (the ranks \(b\) and \(n - b + 1\) of the two order statistics); and notes (when the rule is met, the reminder that a sequential procedure covers the median less often than stated; when there are too few observations, how many are needed; otherwise empty).

Details

The function does not collect data and keeps no state. Call it after each new observation (or batch), starting once seq_blci_dfr_median_pilot observations are in hand, and stop sampling the first time attr(out, "is_satisfied") is TRUE.

With the \(n\) observations sorted as \(X_{(1)} \le \dots \le X_{(n)}\), the interval is \([X_{(b)},\ X_{(n-b+1)}]\). For a continuous distribution it covers the median exactly when the number of observations below the median, a binomial count with \(n\) trials and probability 1/2, lies between \(b\) and \(n - b\). The rank \(b\) starts from the continuity corrected normal approximation to that binomial, \(b = \max\{1, \lceil (n - z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{n} - 1)/2 \rceil\}\), and is lowered if necessary until the exact binomial coverage is at least conf_level. (At confidence levels of 0.80 and above the approximation needed no lowering for any \(n\) up to 3,000; at lower levels it is occasionally short by a small amount.) At the 90%, 95%, and 99% levels this is the largest rank with that property, that is, the narrowest such interval, at more than 97% of the sample sizes up to 2,000, and one rank lower at the rest. Sampling stops at the first \(n\) (at or beyond the pilot size) at which \(X_{(n-b+1)} - X_{(b)} \le 2d\). Unlike the fixed width intervals for a mean, this interval is not symmetric about the point estimate and its length is not fixed in advance; \(2d\) is an upper bound on it.

Minimum sample size. Below a certain sample size no pair of order statistics can reach the confidence level: even the interval from the smallest to the largest observation has coverage \(1 - 2^{1-n}\) (0.50, 0.75, 0.875, and 0.9375 for \(n\) = 2 to 5). With fewer than that many observations (6 at 95%), the rule is reported as not met, the limits and the interval length are NA, and a note says how many observations are needed. attr(out, "min_n") holds that number.

The confidence level is asymptotic, and the shortfall is not small. At any fixed \(n\) the interval has at least the stated coverage. The sequential procedure, however, stops when the interval happens to be short, and short intervals miss the median more often, so its coverage is below the stated level and approaches it only slowly as d shrinks. In simulation (the pilot of seq_blci_dfr_median_pilot() with its defaults, 40,000 replications in each condition, Monte Carlo standard error at most 0.002), with d chosen so that the sample size needed (\(n^*\) in the Details of seq_blci_dfr_median_pilot) was 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, and 800, a nominal 0.95 interval covered the median with probability 0.936, 0.928, 0.926, 0.929, 0.935, and 0.938 for standard normal data, 0.947, 0.925, 0.918, 0.925, 0.929, and 0.937 for unit exponential data, and 0.947, 0.937, 0.936, 0.936, 0.938, and 0.937 for standard Cauchy data. The average final sample size was between 0.94 and 1.05 times \(n^*\) once \(n^*\) was 100 or more. Expect coverage of roughly 0.92 to 0.94 from a nominal 0.95 interval, unless the pilot is already a large part of the sample size needed. The shortfall is larger at a lower level and smaller at a higher one: for the same three distributions with \(n^*\) of 50, 100, 200, and 800, a nominal 0.90 gave between 0.842 and 0.879 and a nominal 0.99 between 0.983 and 0.989. Because the shortfall is not negligible, a check whose rule is met carries a note saying so, which print() shows.

If the stated level must be met, ask for more than is needed. With d held at the value for which the 0.95 procedure needs about 100 and about 400 observations (normal data; 20,000 replications at the first target and 6,000 at the second, standard error at most 0.003), a nominal 0.96 was not enough (coverage 0.941 and 0.948). A nominal 0.97 gave 0.955 and 0.962, with an average final sample size of 1.20 and 1.17 times those 100 and 400 observations, and a nominal 0.975 gave 0.961 and 0.970, at 1.29 and 1.25 times as many. For exponential data at the first of the two targets, a nominal 0.97 gave 0.952.

Ties and constant data. Ties are permitted. With heavily tied data the two order statistics can coincide, giving an interval of length zero; that is a valid (if uninformative about precision) interval for the median of a discrete population, and the rule is then met. (This procedure estimates no variance, so the package's rule for a variance estimate that cannot be used does not arise here.)

References

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

seq_blci_dfr_median_pilot; seq_fwd_dfr_mean for a fixed width interval for a mean.

Other seq_blci_dfr_median: seq_blci_dfr_median_pilot()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Median household income in a district (thousands of dollars), with an
# interval no longer than 10 thousand, 95% confidence. Incomes are right
# skewed; simulated here from a lognormal distribution.
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_blci_dfr_median_pilot(d = 5, conf_level = 0.95)
income <- rlnorm(m, meanlog = log(60), sdlog = 0.5)
out <- seq_blci_dfr_median(income, d = 5, conf_level = 0.95)
out
#> Sequential check (bounded length confidence interval (distribution free))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 10
#>   Criterion n     : NA
#>   Target width    : 10
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 31.4192
#>   median            : 51.19733
#>   upper_limit       : 87.24341
#>   interval_length   : 55.82421
#>   current_n         : 10
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# Add one household at a time until the stopping rule is met. The note
# printed with the result is a reminder that a completed sequential
# procedure covers the median somewhat less often than the stated 95%
# (see Details).
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  income <- c(income, rlnorm(1, meanlog = log(60), sdlog = 0.5))
  out <- seq_blci_dfr_median(income, d = 5, conf_level = 0.95)
}
out
#> Sequential check (bounded length confidence interval (distribution free))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 199
#>   Criterion n     : NA
#>   Target width    : 10
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 56.09514
#>   median            : 60.46713
#>   upper_limit       : 65.82721
#>   interval_length   : 9.732074
#>   current_n         : 199
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
#> 
#>   Note: The confidence level holds for a sample size fixed in advance.
#>         A sequential procedure that stops at this check covers the
#>         median less often than stated: in simulation, about 0.84 to
#>         0.88 for a nominal 0.90, 0.92 to 0.94 for 0.95, and 0.98 to
#>         0.99 for 0.99. See the Details of ?seq_blci_dfr_median.

# Too few observations for 95% confidence: not met, with a note.
seq_blci_dfr_median(income[1:4], d = 5, conf_level = 0.95)
#> Sequential check (bounded length confidence interval (distribution free))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 4
#>   Criterion n     : NA
#>   Target width    : 10
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : NA
#>   median            : 75.69022
#>   upper_limit       : NA
#>   interval_length   : NA
#>   current_n         : 4
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE
#> 
#>   Note: With 4 observations no order statistic interval for the median
#>         can reach 95% confidence (at least 6 are needed), so the
#>         stopping rule is reported as not met. Collect more data and
#>         check again.
